CAF.story:
In December 2013 France sent soldiers to the Central African Republic in Operation Sangaris, under French and not UN command. Six boys aged 9 to 13 later told UN staff that French soldiers had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the camp for displaced people at M'Poko airport in Bangui, in exchange for food rations. The UN did not pass its internal report to the French authorities, and Anders Kompass, the UN official who did, was suspended and resigned in 2016. The Paris prosecutor's investigation grew to cover accusations by 15 children, but in January 2018 French judges closed the case for lack of sufficient evidence, and no soldier was charged.

The UN's own mission, MINUSCA, faced similar accusations. Under UN rules, only the country that sends a peacekeeper can prosecute them, and the UN can only send soldiers home. Two allegations about Gabonese and Burundian troops in Dékoa led to interviews with about 136 alleged victims, 48% of all victims the UN recorded worldwide in 2016. Press reports said 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges. In 2015 girls in Bambari told Human Rights Watch they had been raped by peacekeepers guarding the airport, and in January 2016 the UN withdrew a battalion from the Democratic Republic of the Congo whose soldiers had been accused of rape. In September 2021 it sent home all of Gabon's units, about 450 soldiers, after more allegations.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in the country: 58 by the CPC coalition of armed groups and 35 by government and pro-government forces. It also verified the abduction of 141 children, most of them for recruitment or sexual violence.

None of the foreign soldiers accused of abusing children in the Central African Republic is recorded here as convicted. The country's own forces are now among those the UN finds abusing girls, and no survey has measured the abuse of children across West and Central Africa.

CHN.story:
China opened intercountry adoption, the adoption of its children by parents in other countries, in 1992. About 160,000 children were sent abroad, most of them to the United States, which issued visas to 87,704 children adopted from China between 1994 and 2014. Between 2002 and 2005 six state orphanages in Hunan province bought babies from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with families in China and abroad. In 2005, 23 officials were fired and three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years in prison. The New Yorker reported that the programme came to depend more and more on abuse, abduction and trafficking, and on 5 September 2024 China ended it, except for adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

From 2017, as hundreds of thousands of Uyghur and other Muslim adults were detained in Xinjiang, the authorities built boarding schools and kindergartens with dormitories. Records showed that more than 400 children in one township had lost both parents to internment or prison, and the BBC reported that children were assessed for "centralised care". The New York Times reported that about 497,000 pupils were enrolled in such schools in 2019. A Xinjiang official denied that the state was caring for large numbers of children without parents.

Girls and women are also brought into China from neighbouring countries and sold as brides. Human Rights Watch reported in 2019 that women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States in Myanmar, many displaced by war, were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to $13,000, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency listed 629 girls and women sold to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. Officials told the AP news agency that the investigation largely stopped because of pressure from officials worried about relations with Beijing, and in October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals.

In 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects reports of online abuse from technology companies, received 9,406 reports for China, compared with 1,933,900 for India, because most American platforms are blocked there. The extent of online abuse of children in China is therefore not known, and the trade in brides from neighbouring countries continues.

GBR.story:
Complaints about Jimmy Savile, a BBC presenter who also raised money for NHS hospitals, first reached the police in 1958. Police investigations during his lifetime, the last by Surrey Police in 2007–09, produced no charges, and in December 2011 after his death the BBC programme Newsnight shelved its own report on him. After an ITV documentary in October 2012, the Metropolitan Police opened Operation Yewtree. Its 2013 report recorded 214 crimes from 1955 to 2009, and 73% of the 450 people who made allegations were under 18 at the time.

Cyril Smith, the Liberal MP for Rochdale from 1972 to 1992, was first reported to the police in 1968, by a pupil who was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man". The Director of Public Prosecutions, the official who decides on prosecutions, advised against charging him in 1970, and reviews in 1998 and 1999 brought no charge. He died in 2010, and in 2012 prosecutors said he should have been charged. In 2020 the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), a national inquiry for England and Wales with legal powers, found no organised network of abusers at Westminster but found "overt and direct deference by police towards powerful people".

In Rotherham, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited by groups of men between 1997 and 2013. It called the failures of the council and South Yorkshire Police "blatant", and three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Telford, a 2022 inquiry found more than 1,000 children exploited over at least 30 years, which agencies had treated as "child prostitution". In 2025 Baroness Casey's national audit found that police records were too poor to measure the scale of this abuse, and the government agreed to a new national inquiry with statutory powers.

IICSA's final report in 2022 made 107 recommendations. The first to be fully carried out, removing the three-year deadline for civil claims over child sexual abuse in England and Wales, took effect in June 2026, and the new inquiry into group-based exploitation is starting with Oldham.

ITA.story:
Italy has never held a national inquiry into the abuse of children in the Catholic Church or other institutions, and there are no official statistics on it. In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference, the body of the country's Catholic bishops, said that under the Lateran concordat, the treaty that governs relations between Italy and the Holy See, its priests have no obligation to report suspected abuse to the police. The victims' group Rete l'Abuso has asked for years for an independent inquiry.

Fr Nicola Corradi was accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009, and the diocese flagged him in 2011. He continued working at the order's school in Luján de Cuyo in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016, and in 2019 a court in Mendoza convicted him of abusing deaf children there and sentenced him to 42 years. Joseph Henn, a priest indicted in Arizona in 2003, went to Italy and avoided extradition, the legal handing over of a suspect to another country, until he was arrested in Rome in May 2019.

Italy is also the destination of a trafficking route for women and girls, most of them from Edo State in Nigeria, who are moved overland through Niger and Libya and then by boat, bound by debts and oaths. The UN migration agency IOM recorded an almost 600 percent rise in potential victims arriving by sea between 2014 and 2017. In Palermo, police arrested 19 alleged members of a cell of Black Axe, a Nigerian confraternity, in 2016 over the exploitation of prostitution and other crimes; a judge convicted 14 in 2018, and in 2019 another court rejected the charge of mafia association against five others. In 2016 Europol, the European Union's police agency, said that at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy.

No national inquiry has counted abuse in Italy's churches and institutions, so its extent is not known. It is also not known how many of the 5,000 migrant children who went missing in Italy were exploited.

NLD.story:
In March 2010 the Catholic Church in the Netherlands set up a commission led by the former minister Wim Deetman to examine abuse by its clergy. Its report in December 2011 identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who had abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 minors had been abused. It found that bishops and church officials had known and followed a policy of "not hanging out the dirty washing". In 2012 a state commission received 800 claims of sexual abuse in children's homes and foster families and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor.

The Netherlands also received thousands of children through intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. About 4,000 came from Sri Lanka in the 1980s, where babies were bought or taken from hospitals and handed to paid "acting mothers" who posed as birth mothers in court. A government committee chaired by Tjibbe Joustra reported in February 2021 that adoptions from Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia and other countries from 1967 to 1997/98 involved serious violations and that the Dutch government had failed for decades to prevent them. On 8 February 2021 the government suspended all intercountry adoption with immediate effect, and in 2024 announced that its citizens would no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad.

In 2018 the Netherlands held 47% of the material removed by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images. Its share fell to 11% in 2025, or 33,788 web addresses, but INHOPE, the international network of reporting hotlines, still ranked it first for confirmed material that year.

The Netherlands has examined abuse in the church, in state care and in adoption, and has closed adoption from abroad. Its share of the abuse material found online has fallen, but Dutch servers still hold more confirmed material than those of any other country in INHOPE's count.

SWE.story:
In February 2011 a Swedish government inquiry reported on abuse and neglect in municipal children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980. It recommended a public apology, which was made at Stockholm City Hall that year, and a payment of SEK 250,000 to each person who had suffered serious abuse. A compensation board opened in 2013, and by July 2015 it had decided just over 4,000 applications and rejected 53% of them, with no right of appeal.

Sweden was also one of the main receiving countries for intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. It took in 9,051 children from South Korea between 1957 and 2005. When South Korea tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia in January 1975, the Swedish ambassador urged it to keep sending children. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body investigating past abuses, found that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with known parents as orphans. Children also came to Sweden from Chile, where many were taken from poor mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, from Sri Lanka in the 1980s, when babies were bought from "baby farms", and from Greece between 1950 and 1975.

After campaigning by Chilean adoptees, Sweden set up an independent inquiry. Its report of 2 June 2025, nearly 1,600 pages long, covered 65 years of adoptions and documented many irregular and illegal adoptions that state authorities had some knowledge of. By then Sweden had stopped adoptions from South Korea.

In 2016 Europol, the European Union's police agency, said that about 1,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Sweden, and that it had evidence some of the children who went missing in Europe had been sexually exploited.

Sweden has examined both its own care system and the adoptions it arranged from abroad, and found that state authorities knew of some of the illegal adoptions. The records for this map give no later account of the 1,000 migrant children who went missing in Sweden.

UKR.story:
Between 2012 and 2015 the US-based group Disability Rights International investigated 33 Ukrainian orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities, and concluded that the orphanage system served traffickers as a way to recruit children. La Strada Ukraine, an anti-trafficking charity, told it that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution was "the most typical scheme", and that sexual exploitation in institutions usually began around age 13, often started by staff. A coordinator for IOM, the UN migration agency, said most documented trafficking cases began in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. In the same period Ukraine sent many children abroad for adoption: 18,612 between 2003 and 2022, and the United States issued visas to 10,544 children adopted from Ukraine from 1994 to 2014.

After Russia's full invasion in February 2022, Russian authorities moved children from occupied areas into Russia. In May 2022 President Vladimir Putin signed a decree that made it easier for Ukrainian children to receive Russian citizenship so that Russian families could adopt them, and Russia paid families for each child. Researchers at Yale University found at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea where at least 6,000 Ukrainian children were held for "re-education". In March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and for Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's children's rights commissioner, for the unlawful deportation and transfer of children. The UN verified the abduction of 122 children by Russian forces and authorities in 2022 and 2023, and a UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces had raped children.

The war also put children left in Ukrainian institutions at risk. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report said children evacuated from at least 195 facilities were at high risk, that officials at several state institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent, and that no complicit official had been convicted for the eighth year running.

By October 2026 Ukraine counted 20,651 children deported or forcibly displaced and 2,752 returned, so most have not come back. Children who remain in Ukraine's institutions are at risk from traffickers, and no official has been convicted of taking part.

VAT.story:
The Holy See is both the central government of the Catholic Church and a state with its own diplomats and courts. In 1922, and again in 1962 in an instruction called Crimen sollicitationis, it ordered that church trials of priests accused of sexual acts with children be kept absolutely secret, on pain of automatic excommunication. In 2001 it required bishops to send every case of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, its office for church discipline, and kept those cases under the pontifical secret, its highest level of confidentiality. Between 2004 and 2013 that office studied 3,420 credible cases and dismissed 884 priests from the priesthood.

In August 2013 it recalled Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, its nuncio, or ambassador, to the Dominican Republic, amid allegations that he had abused minors, before Dominican prosecutors opened their investigation. He was charged by a Vatican prosecutor in 2015 and died before trial. In 2017 it recalled Mgr Carlo Capella from its embassy in Washington, and in 2018 its own court convicted him of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years; he was not tried in the United States or Canada. Archbishop Luigi Ventura, its nuncio to France, was tried in Paris in his absence and in December 2020 received an eight-month suspended sentence. Ireland's Murphy Commission, a state inquiry, received no files from the Vatican.

In 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said the Holy See had placed the church's reputation and the protection of offenders above children's interests and had moved abusive priests to new parishes. In 2019 Pope Francis required clergy to report suspected abuse to church authorities, though not to the police, and in December 2019 he lifted the pontifical secret so that case files could be given to state authorities.

Since December 2019 church files on abuse can be given to state authorities, but the Holy See still decides whether to hand them over, and its own rules do not require clergy to report abuse to the police.
